newsitem.title: FRANCE: Galliano triumphs with romantic couture for Dior.
newsitem.headline: Galliano triumphs with romantic couture for Dior.

text.p: Britain's John Galliano married tradition with his own romantic twist in his first collection for Christian Dior, triumphantly taking the fashion set on a Proustian voyage down the boulevards of pre-World War One Paris.

In the second event of the spring summer haute couture season following Alexander McQueen's anti-climactic debut for Givenchy, Galliano sent out a stunning series of skinny Belle Epoque gowns, their derrieres padded and narrow skirts flaring gracefully from the knee to the floor.

In bias-cut pistachio satin trimmed with mink and chinoiserie embroideries -- and matching mink-trimmed sandals -- or mauve silk covered with black chantilly this was ultimate Galliano splendour paired with the skill of Dior's atelier.
It was a fitting celebration for the house's 50th anniversary.

Thousands of pink and white roses overflowed from Grecian vases as the fashion community invaded the entire ground floor of a luxury hotel to watch Galliano faithfully send out Dior's New Look suits, in trademark Prince of Wales tweeds, but with skirts clipped high on the thigh.

Then came Masai beaded breast plates on a sleek, wasp-waisted black cocktail dress and the astonishing spread of champagne tulle-ruffled ballgown with miniature roses embroidered on its velveteen bustier.
Beads reappeared as the colourful corset of a curvy black taffeta column, the breastplate of a sheer mesh top over sleek satin evening trousers or the straps of high-heeled sandals.

The swashbuckling young designer was switched from LVMH sister house Givenchy after just a year to replace Gianfranco Ferre at Dior in October, as part of LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault's strategy to dust off the old label by entrusting it to one of fashion's greatest imaginations and craftsmen.
In homage to one of Dior's first models, Mitzah Bricard, there were little leopard print slip dresses with lilac lace.

"It was a really great collection," said menswear designer Paul Smith. "He managed to mix pure Galliano with pure Dior, successfully incorporating both styles, especially with those black and white plaids."
The Duchess of York, Sarah Ferguson, said she loved the show but would not be buying any of the dresses. "It was absolutely excellent, really fascinating. I'm a great admirerer," she said.

Earlier, Emanuel Ungaro remained faithful to his time-worn formula of sellable, wearable Parisian chic, pairing slim, nubby, multi-coloured tweed jackets with sparkled threading over cheetah print, liquid chiffon jumpsuits of emerald, plum and powder pink.

Straight and narrow coats of ivory, coral or navy wool topped floral dresses of lame chiffon in perky floral prints. But the strongest items were the simplest: bias cut creamy crepe sheaths. The animal motif chiffons returned for evening, long, slender and backless.
Four big ball gowns came with tiered, petticoated skirting.
With a skewer of actresses in his front row, Ungaro succeeded in creating the stir that his clothes failed to: Jane Birkin, Marthe Keller, Charlotte Rampling and Anouk Aimee.

"I don't know Ungaro's work and I came here to discover it," said Rampling from behind her dark glasses. "I was very moved, it was extremely feminine, extremely glamourous. It's not really my style but I realise there's a different way of dressing."
